items.text: Late autism diagnosis has a name for what happens after: biographical illumination. Your whole past reorganises. Relief and grief arrive together. Neither cancels the other. What part of yours rewrote itself first?
items.rationale: Names the PubMed 2026-sourced concept precisely, which does the emotional legitimising work automatically — especially for the grief, which people suppress because they feel they should just be grateful. The closing question earns engagement honestly.

items.text: The grief after a late autism diagnosis doesn't mean you're ungrateful. It means you're mourning years lived without context. Both are true. You're allowed to hold them at the same time.
items.rationale: Targets the guilt that shadows post-diagnosis grief — a specific emotional trap rarely named directly. Distinct from the first post by focusing on the grief/gratitude tension rather than the biographical-reorganisation concept.

items.text: 91% of neurodivergent workers mask at work. That's not social awkwardness management — it's a second job. No pay, no breaks, no sick days. Running on top of the actual job.
items.rationale: Opens with the sourced stat, then delivers the sharpest labour-frame reframe of masking in the briefing. Each clause earns its place. Immediately quotable without exaggerating the claim.

items.text: Masking draws from the same cognitive pool as executive function. Every hour spent managing how you appear is an hour your brain can't spend on the actual work. That's not a personal failing — that's just math.
items.rationale: Deepens the masking angle with a mechanism, not a stat — explains why masking is exhausting rather than asserting that it is. The 'that's just math' close removes self-blame cleanly without being dismissive.

items.text: Spending years feeling half-right in ADHD spaces and half-right in autistic spaces — too impulsive for one, too rigid for the other — that dissonance has a name. AuDHD isn't additive. It's its own profile.
items.rationale: Directly names the 'half-right' identity experience without reducing it to a clinical list. The research-backed final claim that the profile is genuinely distinct gives the validation something solid to stand on.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Too impulsive / too rigid' uses deficit-adjacent descriptors — framed here as subjective felt experience, not clinical judgment. Monitor responses; could soften to 'too scattered / too structured' in a follow-up if the framing gets pushback.

items.text: Not all demand avoidance is PDA. Demand avoidance can come from anxiety, executive dysfunction, or trauma. PDA is a specific profile. The distinction matters — different experiences call for different support.
items.rationale: Stays purely clarifying — no sides taken, no dismissal of PDA, no suggestion demand avoidance is trivial. Short, declarative, and practically useful for self-understanding and for parents trying to understand their kids.
items.sensitivity_flag: PDA has contested standing in some professional and community circles. Post takes no position on diagnostic validity, only distinguishes concepts — but the topic may attract debate. Watch replies and don't wade in defensively.

items.text: Your nervous system isn't fragile. It has a narrower window of tolerance — that's wiring, not weakness. Dysregulation isn't a character flaw. It's neurology. And neurology responds to environment, not willpower.
items.rationale: Counters the internalised 'why can't I just handle this?' shame loop directly. The final clause pivots from explanation to agency — environment can be shaped — without tipping into self-improvement or fix-yourself framing.

items.text: Regulation tools aren't self-improvement exercises. For an autistic nervous system, they're infrastructure. You're not trying to be better — you're making the environment carry a load it was always supposed to share.
items.rationale: A second Angle 5 post with a distinct frame: shifts from 'your wiring isn't a flaw' to 'these tools aren't about fixing you.' Removes the self-improvement connotation that makes many autistic people resistant to regulation strategies.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't giving up. For PDA kids, conventional compliance-based approaches activate a genuine threat response. Reducing demands is how you bring the system back online. That's strategy, not surrender.
items.rationale: Addresses the 'you're capitulating' criticism PDA parents face head-on, then flips it with a mechanism, not just a slogan. The sourced finding about threat response gives the reframe something concrete to stand on.

items.text: One change that costs nothing: ditch overhead lighting when you can. Lamps at eye level or below. Your nervous system processes that light as input, not ambience. Let the room carry some of the load.
items.rationale: Concrete, low-demand, immediately actionable. Frames the tweak as nervous-system support, not productivity advice. The final line echoes the broader environmental-load theme without over-explaining it.

items.text: The disclosure decision doesn't happen once. It reopens every new job, every new manager, every new team. That ongoing calculus is its own burnout driver. How do you carry it?
items.rationale: Names a specific, under-articulated cognitive and emotional load without overstating it. The closing question is open enough to generate genuine responses across different disclosure strategies — not a poll, a conversation.

items.text: What's the one environmental change that made the biggest difference for your nervous system — at home or at work? Lighting, sound, layout, temperature. Genuinely curious what's worked.
items.rationale: Opens a practical community exchange without manufacturing urgency or a cliffhanger. Pairs with the two practical posts to seed replies with real-world knowledge — which also directly informs future content angles.
